DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study for Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

The study is clearly structured and most of its arithmetic is correct. But the pilot data contradict three central claims made by the study and its author: that participation held up across houses and flats, that treatment is local, and that the service is fully funded. As written, the recommendation is not supported by the evidence. Cabinet should not approve it in this form.

## Critical issues

### 1. Participation did not hold up across housing types

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses, and their yield per participating household was lower (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

Section 2 says participation "was broadly similar across housing types," and Section 7 repeats that conclusion. The data show the opposite. This is the main justification for a "single, simple service" with no separate approach for flats, so that conclusion falls with it. About 10,400 of the district's households (20%) are flats. The pilot shows they need a different approach, such as communal bins, bin-store access, or targeted engagement, and that approach needs a budget.

### 2. The district projection uses a participation rate the pilot did not produce

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%** (2,280 of 4,000). The 64% figure does not appear anywhere in the pilot results.

The pilot's 20% flats share matches the district's, so 57% is directly applicable. Recalculated tonnage:

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| As stated (64% × 1.9 kg) | ~3,290 t |
| Pilot overall rate (57% × 1.9 kg) | ~2,930 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | ~2,870 t |

Tonnage is overstated by about 13–15%, and the disposal saving is overstated by the same proportion.

### 3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage

Section 4 states that Brookfield will provide **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection of about 2,870 t is well above that, and the study's own 3,290 t figure is nearly double it.

The study does not say where the remaining 1,100–1,500 t would go. The only alternative mentioned is a plant 46 miles away. That would add haulage or transfer costs, and possibly a different gate fee, and none of these are costed. The author's statement that "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is therefore true for only part of the tonnage until 2029.

### 4. The service is not fully funded on the study's own evidence

The £520,000 provisional allocation covers the stated £490,000 net cost with only about £30,000 to spare. Correcting the errors above removes that margin:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t) | £243,000 | £490,400 | +£29,600 |
| Corrected tonnage (~2,870 t at £74/t) | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 | **–£1,000** |
| Only 1,800 t diverted at the £74 saving (remainder not costed) | ~£133,000 | ~£600,000 | **–£80,000** |

Any extra cost for handling tonnage above Brookfield's capacity widens the gap further.

The funding is also described as "provisional" and as something the Government "has indicated." The study presents it as certain. It should include a sensitivity analysis and state what happens if the final allocation is lower or time-limited.

## Significant issues

### 5. The cost base is incomplete

The author calls the analysis "complete," but it omits several items:
- **Haulage or transfer costs** for tonnage that goes beyond Brookfield.
- **Absence and holiday cover**, and any spare vehicle. Six vehicles and six crews leaves no resilience.
- **Supervision, management, and the dedicated phone line and web page** described in Section 6.
- **Capital and cash flow.** Vehicles cost £990,000 up front, and caddies for 52,000 households are an up-front cost too. Only depreciation is shown, with no financing cost.
- **Liner policy after the first three months.** The study should state whether liners will be supplied indefinitely and whether that ongoing cost is in the £88,000 line.

The study also does not say whether £34,000 per operative includes employer on-costs.

### 6. The pilot evidence is weaker than presented

- **Satisfaction:** 81% is of "surveyed" households. The study gives no response rate. If respondents were mainly participants, the figure overstates satisfaction across the pilot population.
- **Novelty effect:** six months is short. Participation commonly falls after launch, yet the projection assumes pilot rates continue indefinitely.
- **Contamination:** "under 2%" comes from spot checks only. The study does not give the sample size or the split between houses and flats.

### 7. The timetable is tight and its risks are not assessed

- Vehicles ordered in December 2026 are expected in March 2027. A lead time of about three months is short for specialist vehicles, and the study gives no supplier confirmation. The author says the timetable "works back from the vehicle lead time," but the study does not state that lead time or its source.
- Cabinet approval must come before the December order deadline. The study does not mention this.
- Crews are recruited from February and trained in March, which leaves about a month to recruit 12 operatives.
- Caddies are delivered to 52,000 households in the same month that the vehicles arrive.

The study has no contingency plan if vehicles or caddies are late.

### 8. The statutory context is missing

The study notes the legal requirement but does not state the deadline that applies to Thornbury. It also does not say whether the April 2027 start depends on a transitional arrangement or represents a compliance risk. Cabinet needs this information to weigh the urgency of the decision.

## Minor points

- In Table 1, the "All" row's 1.9 kg/household is a rounded weighted average (about 1.86 kg). It should be shown to two decimal places or footnoted.
- The £74/t saving assumes residual collection costs do not change. It would help to state this or to estimate any savings from residual rounds.

## Recommended changes before Cabinet

1. Correct Section 2's statement about participation by housing type and propose a costed approach for flats.
2. Recalculate tonnage using the pilot's actual rates by housing type.
3. Secure and cost treatment for all projected tonnage up to 2029, or explain how tonnage above 1,800 t will be handled.
4. Re-run the financial case with the corrected tonnage, the missing cost lines, and sensitivity to the final funding allocation.
5. Confirm the vehicle lead time with suppliers and add a risk register and contingency plan to the implementation section.
6. Change the Section 7 recommendation so it no longer states that the service is "fully funded" or can be delivered "on a uniform basis" until these points are resolved.
